title: Ang 1327–1332: Prabhati begins
hook: Guru Nanak opens the dawn raga
tomorrow: first morning in the dorm, and Hana's alarm rings before dawn. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang 1319: Kalyan, the short evening raga, and God as father and mother in one breath. Peace past the end of the driveway. The night is over now. Here's the dawn.
screen: `FATHER AND MOTHER, ONE BREATH.` → `NOW, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Five in the morning. The car is packed to the roof, Harjit is checking the tires with a flashlight, and someone knocks. It's Maya, in pajama pants and a hoodie, holding a thermos and a card. I wasn't letting you leave without me, she says. Inside the card, in her grandmother's shaky handwriting, is a line from a psalm about the morning. Simran reads it under the porch light, and it sounds a lot like Bebe's alarm.
screen: `FIVE A.M., THE CAR PACKED.` → `MAYA, A THERMOS, A CARD.` → `A PSALM ABOUT THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: So why get up before the world does? Prabhati, the dawn raga, begins on ang 1327, and Guru Nanak opens it. In paraphrase: by your Name we cross over; your Name is honor, your Name is worship. Sikhs call the hours before dawn amrit vela, from Guru Nanak's Japji: in the ambrosial hours, reflect on the true Name and its greatness. That's the tradition's answer. Meet the Name first, before the day can introduce itself. Now the card. Maya's grandmother copied out Psalm 5, in the King James words: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.” Here's what they share. Both give God the very first hour, before the phone, before the traffic, while it's still dark. And here's an honest difference. In this psalm, the morning is for setting out a prayer, then looking up, watching for the answer. In Prabhati's opening and in amrit vela, the morning is for the Name itself: remembering it, praising it, crossing over by it. One lays out a request and watches the sky. The other fills the first hour with the Name. Here's something to tell a friend tonight: two families, two books, and the same alarm before sunrise. Maya hugs her too hard. The car pulls out with the porch light still on.
screen: `PRABHATI: THE DAWN RAGA.` · `BY YOUR NAME WE CROSS OVER.` · `AMRIT VELA, AND PSALM FIVE.` · `SHARED HOUR, DIFFERENT MORNING.` · then, large: `DAWN.`

segments.voice: Whatever time it is where you are, treat this sit as the first hour. If you pray, you can repeat Waheguru softly with each breath, the practice Sikhs call simran. If not, let each breath be the first thing you meet, before any screen.
Ang 1327. Where Prabhati begins: Guru Nanak opens the dawn raga with the Name as the way across.
Hold onto this: dawn, when the Name comes before the day does. Drive safe, Simran.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep amrit vela rise before dawn to bathe, recite the morning prayers and remember the Name; Prabhati hymns are sung in kirtan in the early morning, with Guru Nanak's at the start of the raga.
